A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Token Sample Complexity of Attention by the same authors. All 44 pages of v1 and 42 pages of v2, including Appendices A–C, support comparison. Text, equations, and figures can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original Gaussian Monte Carlo simulations and BERT experiments on WikiText/Wikipedia, with results in Figures 1–5.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C.7 report original Gaussian simulations and BigBird experiments on text distributions. Figure 1 also presents an original token-embedding visualization.

M1.justification: Both versions analyze the same softmax self-attention operator, mean-field formulation, multihead extension, and hardmax limit. Changes from Gamma/mu notation to f/nu and from ARC to ATC do not alter the procedure. BERT and BigBird are experimental subjects, not newly proposed methods.

E1.justification: V1's real-text evaluation concerns English WikiText/Wikipedia. V2 additionally evaluates German and Chinese Wikipedia and CC-News, substantially broadening language and domain coverage. Gaussian data and English encyclopedic text remain represented.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing algorithms against a proposed method. Both compare empirical convergence with theoretical rate curves. The BERT-to-BigBird substitution changes the studied architecture, while the newly discussed Boursier–Boyer work is not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The reported real-data setup changes from BERT-base-uncased with 1M/20M reference tokens and subsamples reaching 10,000/200,000 tokens to BigBird–RoBERTa–base with positional interpolation, approximately 500,000 reference tokens per source, and subsamples of 1,000–3,000. V1's one-dimensional Gaussian example at fixed horizon 0.03 is replaced by a four-dimensional horizon sweep with covariance 0.1I.

E4.justification: V1's controlled BERT attention-matrix rescaling and detailed headwise analyses are removed. V2 examines language/domain differences in horizon-dependent slowdown, adds selected German-layer convergence curves, and introduces a t-SNE illustration of support coverage. The higher-dimensional Gaussian horizon-sensitivity analysis is retained in Appendix C.7.1.

E5.justification: V1 reports 200 or 20 repetitions for its BERT settings and labels uncertainty as 95% confidence intervals. V2 specifies 500 repetitions and ±3 standard-error bars for the new BigBird curves in Figures 4 and 7. Retained Gaussian panels keep their 95% intervals. These changes do not establish additional runs of the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: The BERT result sets and one-dimensional Gaussian error curves are replaced by BigBird and four-dimensional Gaussian results. For example, v2 Figure 4 reports absolute mean-convergence exponents 0.47, 0.41, and 0.33 for German layers 5, 1, and 0. These are different experimental conditions, not same-setting improvements. V1 Figure 2's Gaussian panels are unchanged in v2 Figure 5.

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem B.11 and its proof for two Dirac masses, claiming matching n^(-1/2) bounds with polynomial support-radius dependence, uniform in query radius. Former Proposition 3.3 becomes an explicitly large-n result with confidence 1−2δ in Proposition C.3. Theorem 5.3's sample-size condition and confidence factors in Appendix B.2 are also revised. The principal convergence exponents otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central claims remain token sample complexity, uniform n^(-1/2) attention-map convergence, slower geometry-dependent moment convergence, and logarithmic Gaussian hardmax convergence. The abstract is essentially unchanged, and the revised experiments continue supporting the same claim of practical sub-parametric behavior.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses non-sharpness for particular distributions and identifies proving Gaussian tightness as an open problem. It adds an explanation involving shared query/key/value randomness and tentatively extends the interpretation beyond i.i.d. tokens. It also corrects the hardmax discussion from logarithmic decay being 'quicker' to 'slower' than polynomial decay.

D1.justification: V2 documents positional interpolation for BigBird and newly states that code is provided in supplementary material. V1's tiled-attention implementation details—chunk size 4,000 and memory usage below 3 GB—are removed, along with its IDRIS resource acknowledgment. The PDFs establish a changed code-access statement, not independently verified code availability.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated comparison with Boursier and Boyer (2025), distinguishing dependent queries/keys/values, moment convergence versus L2 error, and Jacobian results. It also adds references for positional interpolation, MMD, and datasets, while dropping several earlier bibliography entries. The broader mean-field positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Related work becomes Section 2; growth, pointwise, compact-support, Gaussian, and detailed hardmax material moves into appendices. Expanded proof sketches occupy Sections 4.3 and 5.3, notation changes throughout, and the experimental narrative and conclusion are rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, adds the introductory t-SNE figure, and replaces BERT multipanel displays with BigBird scatterplots and selected convergence curves. Identical higher-dimensional Gaussian panels move from v1 Figure 2 to appendix Figure 5 with a revised caption. Figure placement, captions, and legends change substantially.

improvement.justification: V2 improves exposition, broadens text coverage, and adds useful qualifications and mathematical corrections. However, it replaces the largest reference sets and subsamples with much smaller ones and introduces a correctness problem: Theorem B.11 claims R0^2/sqrt(n) bounds, while Equation (17) at x=0 gives binomial sampling error of order R0/sqrt(n), incompatible with the stated uniform radius scaling. These substantive benefits and harms prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
